title: U.S.-India Insight: India’s Trade Deals: Only a Starting Point to Progress
gist: Post-FTA data show India's goods trade with Australia (+76%) and the UAE (+81%) grew sharply, but neither partner gained meaningful share of India's total trade (Australia ~2%, UAE 7%->8%). CSIS concludes trade deals are no shortcut: India needs land, labor, power, water and judicial reforms, after protectionist 'Make in India' left manufacturing stuck at 13-15% of GDP.

insights.claim: India-Australia goods trade averaged about $13b a year in FY20-FY21 before their trade agreement and about $23b a year in FY25-FY26, a 76% increase, with Indian exports doubling from $4b to $8b annually.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Shows meaningful bilateral trade growth after India's FTAs, relevant for exporters in both countries.
insights.quote: This marks a 76% increase in average annual trade. India’s average exports doubled from $4b annually to $8b annually during this period.

insights.claim: India-UAE goods trade averaged $55b a year in FY20-FY21 and $100b a year in FY25-FY26, an 81% increase, with Indian exports rising from $22b to $36b annually.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: The UAE corridor is a fast-growing trade relationship for India.
insights.quote: In the most recent 2 fiscal years (FY25 & FY26), India-UAE total goods trade averaged $100b a year. This marks an 81% increase in average annual trade.

insights.claim: Despite strong growth, Australia remains around 2% of India's total trade and the UAE rose only from about 7% to 8%, meaning FTAs did not materially shift India's trade mix.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Headline FTA growth may largely reflect overall trade growth; temper expectations for deal-driven export booms.
insights.quote: neither country has substantially gained ground in terms of India’s total trade mix

insights.claim: There is no evidence that India's trade agreements caused a flood of imports, but also little evidence they produce quick relative export wins with partners.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Reduces political risk of FTA backlash in India while signaling modest near-term economic upside.
insights.quote: there is no evidence supporting older Indian fears about trade agreements causing a flood of imports

insights.claim: India's recent and upcoming trade agreements with EFTA, Oman, the UK, New Zealand and the EU came into force in 2024-25 or will in the year ahead.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: A wave of new Indian market-access deals is opening, though gains may be gradual.
insights.quote: Many others have followed including the Swiss-led EFTA block, Oman, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, and the European Union.

themes.theme: India trade policy history and reform needs

insights.claim: India's aggressive trade-deal push is often seen as a response to Trump-era US trade uncertainty, but it began before Trump's second term; US policy is at most an accelerant.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: India's FTA strategy is structural, not merely reactive, so likely to persist regardless of US policy.
insights.quote: While this may be an accelerant, India’s vigorous pursuit of deals started well before President Trump’s second term.
insights.locator: India’s more aggressive approach to signing

insights.claim: India's 2000-2011 trade deals with Asian neighbors such as Japan, Korea and ASEAN were more political statements than economic breakthroughs, with large exclusion lists and slow tariff cuts; India then signed few deals for a decade and exited RCEP in 2019.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Context for judging the depth of India's new-generation agreements.
insights.quote: the deals themselves are more “political statements” than groundbreaking economic measures
insights.locator: India had a modestly aggressive trade policy

insights.claim: The Modi government's protectionist 'Make in India' tariffs and non-tariff barriers from 2014 led to relative stagnation, with manufacturing stuck at 13-15% of GDP over the last decade per the World Bank.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Protectionism failed to lift Indian manufacturing; the pivot to PLI subsidies and FTAs is the new bet.
insights.quote: The net result, per the World Bank, has been relative stagnation, with manufacturing hovering at 13% to 15% of GDP over the last decade.
insights.locator: Our program has noted many times

insights.claim: India needs difficult domestic reforms in land, labor, power, water and judicial remediation to realize gains from its trade agreements; there are no shortcuts.
insights.speaker: CSIS
insights.so_what: Domestic reform progress is the key variable for India's export competitiveness and manufacturing investment case.
insights.quote: Pushing ahead with difficult reforms in areas like land, labor, power, water, and judicial remediation will help India fulfill the promise of these new agreements.
